# Introduction

Retrosynthesis guides the planning of chemical synthesis by working backward from a target molecule to simpler precursors until suitable starting materials are reached. In template-based retrosynthesis, reaction templates describe where a chemical transformation can occur and how atoms and bonds should be rearranged to generate candidate precursors. These templates combine molecular patterns with instructions for modifying the matched structure. In practice, SMARTS is used to describe molecular patterns, while Reaction SMARTS and the related SMIRKS notation use atom-mapped patterns to specify chemical transformations [@daylight_smarts; @daylight_smirks].

A reaction template can match several positions within a target molecule, potentially generating different precursors at each position. Identifying these matches alone is therefore insufficient to describe the possible retrosynthetic transformations. For each match, the template atoms must be mapped to the corresponding target atoms, the specified changes applied, and the resulting structure separated into precursor molecules. The number of hydrogen atoms and aromaticity must also be updated. Each precursor must retain a link to the target, template, and individual reaction application that produced it. Together, these steps generate the molecular structures and relationships needed to assemble successive transformations into complete retrosynthetic routes.

At each step of a retrosynthetic search, newly generated molecules form a search frontier for further expansion. This frontier can contain thousands of molecules, and evaluating each against thousands of reaction templates creates millions of molecule–template pairs. Learned models therefore rank templates and restrict their application to the most promising candidates [@segler2018planning; @genheden2020aizynthfinder; @chen2020retrostar]. Guided search methods, including Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) [@segler2018planning] and A* [@chen2020retrostar], likewise prioritize promising routes, but each expansion still requires applying reaction templates and constructing precursors. Faster reaction application can allow a planner to examine more branches, explore longer routes, or retain more alternatives within a fixed time. It can also support ranking after successful transformations have been generated, using information from both the target and its precursors. Complete enumeration remains useful for validating implementations, characterizing workloads, and bounded exploration, particularly with compact, curated rule collections.

Most reaction-template implementations are CPU based. RDKit compiles Reaction SMARTS and applies the encoded transformations through RunReactants [@rdkit; @rdkit_book], while RDChiral adds stereochemical handling and post-processing tailored to retrosynthesis [@coley2019rdchiral]. Indigo [@pavlov2011indigo; @indigo_reaction_api], the Chemistry Development Kit [@willighagen2017cdk; @cdk2_12; @cdk_smirks_api], Open Babel [@oboyle2011openbabel; @openbabel_chemtsfm], CDPKit [@cdpkit; @cdpkit_chem_api], and Chython [@chython2_18; @chython_reactor_api] provide related SMARTS- or SMIRKS-based transformations with varying semantics. Given the size of the search frontier and the number of templates evaluated for each molecule, moving reaction-template application to GPUs could accelerate retrosynthetic expansion.

Current GPU implementations address only individual stages of the reaction-application pipeline. nvMolKit performs batched SMARTS substructure matching on NVIDIA GPUs and returns the corresponding atom mappings [@nvmolkit0_6; @nvmolkit_substructure_api]. GSI, cuTS, SIGMo, and Δ-Motif accelerate related subgraph-matching or subgraph-isomorphism tasks [@zeng2020gsi; @lee2021cuts; @decaro2025sigmo; @wang2026deltamotif], while general-purpose GPU graph algorithms support connected-component identification and chordless-cycle enumeration [@jaiganesh2018connected; @dias2014chordless]. However, these methods do not integrate match enumeration, graph modification, precursor separation, and the recalculation of chemical properties into a complete GPU reaction-application pipeline.

Here, we present {{< meta libname >}}, a reaction-template application library with dedicated NVIDIA CUDA and Apple Metal backends and a parallel CPU backend developed primarily as a reference. To our knowledge, {{< meta libname >}} is the first implementation of the complete reaction-template application pipeline on GPUs. The library processes batches of molecular graphs and returns precursors with records linking each to its source product, template, and reaction application. Within a synthesis planner, molecular identity handling, stock lookup, deduplication, and route search remain separate components. This modular design allows GPU-generated precursor batches to be reused in subsequent expansion steps, while compact molecular keys support CPU-side stock lookup, deduplication, and route search.

We evaluate {{< meta libname >}} by measuring template compatibility and the agreement of molecular keys and precursor outputs across backends and against RDKit- and RDChiral-based references. We also test whether generated precursors remain usable during multi-step template-guided replay, report absolute performance on specified hardware and software configurations, and quantify the workload generated by depth-bounded exhaustive expansion over a large template collection. This evaluation spans individual reaction applications, successive route steps, and integration into a broader retrosynthetic expansion workflow. VeSMA is released as reusable cheminformatics infrastructure for integration into larger retrosynthetic workflows and for independent inspection, benchmarking, and extension.
